items.stem: You may have noticed that fibres of coconut husk are hard and brittle, whereas the leaf stalks of coriander are soft and flexible. Find out the reason.
items.answer: The difference in texture and flexibility is due to the distinct types of simple permanent tissues present in them. The fibres of a coconut husk are made of sclerenchyma tissue, which consists of dead cells with thick, lignified walls that make them hard and brittle. In contrast, the leaf stalks of coriander contain collenchyma tissue, which consists of living cells with unevenly thickened corners that provide mechanical support along with flexibility.

items.stem: Why do you think that a thick cuticle on the outer wall of epidermis is advantageous for a plant living in the desert but disadvantageous for a plant living underwater?
items.answer: A thick cuticle is highly advantageous for a desert plant because it acts as a waterproof waxy layer that significantly reduces water loss through transpiration in hot, dry environments. However, this same thick cuticle would be disadvantageous for an underwater plant. Aquatic plants do not face the risk of dehydration and need to easily exchange dissolved gases directly with the surrounding water, a process that a thick waxy layer would obstruct. Therefore, an aquatic plant benefits from having little to no cuticle to facilitate efficient diffusion.

items.stem: Once water is absorbed by plant roots, it has to travel against gravity through xylem. How do the ‘dead’ cells of the xylem work together with the living cells of leaves at the top to keep the water moving?
items.answer: The dead tubular cells of the xylem, such as tracheids and vessels, act as continuous physical pipes that allow water to flow upwards from the roots. The living cells in the leaves contribute to this process by losing water through stomata in a process called transpiration. This evaporation from the leaves creates a suction force, or transpiration pull, which continuously draws the column of water up through the dead, thick- walled xylem vessels against the force of gravity. Thus, the living leaf cells provide the pulling force while the dead xylem cells provide the necessary structural pathway. Tissues in Action

items.stem: What do you think will happen if there were no stomata in the epidermis of the stem or leaves?
items.answer: If there were no stomata in the epidermis, the plant would be unable to perform gaseous exchange, thereby halting the critical processes of photosynthesis and respiration. Furthermore, without stomata, transpiration could not occur, meaning the plant could not generate the transpiration pull required to transport water and minerals upward from the roots.

items.stem: Look at the picture given below. Carefully observe the various poses of classical and folk dances of India. Can you identify which joints are involved? Also, what type of movement each joint allows?
items.answer: The dancers use several distinct joints to achieve these dynamic poses. The ball and socket joints in the shoulders and hips are highly involved, allowing for forward, backward, sideways, and circular movements of the arms and legs. The hinge joints in the elbows, knees, and ankles permit the bending and straightening of limbs in a single direction, while the pivot joint in the neck allows the head to smoothly move from side to side. items.stem: Meristematic tissues divide repeatedly. What property of their cells allows them to do this? (i) They have thick walls for protection. (ii) They contain large vacuoles that store nutrients. (iii) They have thin walls, dense cytoplasm and large prominent nucleus. (iv) They are functionally differentiated cells.
items.answer: (iii) They have thin walls, dense cytoplasm and large prominent nucleus. Meristematic cells are actively dividing, requiring thin walls for easy division, dense cytoplasm to support high metabolic rates, and a large nucleus to coordinate continuous cell cycles, while lacking large vacuoles that would hinder division.

items.stem: If a plant is unable to transport food from leaves to roots which tissue is malfunctioning? (i) Xylem (ii) Phloem (iii) Epidermis (iv) Sclerenchyma
items.answer: (ii) Phloem Phloem is the complex permanent conducting tissue specifically responsible for transporting the food prepared in the leaves to all other parts of the plant, including the roots.

items.stem: Why are the epithelial tissues that line an animal’s internal organs usually only one or a few cells thick? (i) To store food efficiently. (ii) To provide maximum strength. (iii) To allow quick exchange of materials across them. (iv) To reduce friction.
items.answer: (iii) To allow quick exchange of materials across them. A thin layer of epithelial cells minimizes the distance for diffusion, facilitating the rapid and efficient exchange of gases, nutrients, and waste products across the lining of internal organs like blood vessels and alveoli.

items.stem: You can perform these two jumps as show in figure Straight-leg jump — keep knees and ankles stiff. Normal jump — bend knees and ankles naturally. How did your ankle, knee and hip positions differ between the two jumps? Click Here to Buy book on Flipkart
items.answer: In the straight-leg jump, the joints at the ankle, knee, and hip are kept rigid and fully extended, preventing the bending required to absorb shock and generate upward force efficiently. In the normal jump, the ankle, knee, and hip joints undergo a coordinated bending (flexion) during the preparatory phase and rapid straightening (extension) to push off the ground. The normal jump utilizes the hinge joints in the knees and the flexibility of the ankles and hips to act like springs for better movement.

items.stem: Which type of joint is involved when you bend your knees and ankles? (i) Ball and socket (ii) Hinge (iii) Pivot
items.answer: (ii) Hinge The knee and ankle joints function primarily as hinge joints, allowing movement back and forth in predominantly one plane (bending and straightening), similar to the opening and closing mechanism of a door.

items.stem: In each of the following cases (A, B, C and D), choose the correct option as given below: (i) Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A). (ii) Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A). (iii) (A) is true, but (R) is false. (iv) (A) is false, but (R) is true. A. Assertion: Epithelium is well-suited for gas exchange in the lungs. Reason: It consists of multiple layers of tall cells that slow down diffusion.
items.answer: (iii) (A) is true, but (R) is false. The epithelium in the lungs (alveoli) is well-suited for gas exchange because it consists of a single, thin layer of flat cells, not multiple layers of tall cells, which would indeed slow down diffusion. B. Assertion: Cardiac muscle can contract continuously without fatigue. Reason: Cardiac muscle cells have a high number of mitochondria and an abundant blood supply.

(i) Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A). Cardiac muscles work tirelessly throughout life, and this continuous rhythmic contraction requires immense energy, which is continuously provided by numerous mitochondria and sustained by a rich blood supply delivering constant oxygen and nutrients. C. Assertion: Tendons connect bone to bone and allow joint movement. Reason: Tendons are made of tough connective tissue that transmits force from muscle to bone.

(iv) (A) is false, but (R) is true. The assertion is false because tendons connect muscles to bones, whereas ligaments connect bone to bone. The reason is a true statement describing the composition and function of tendons in facilitating movement. D. Assertion: In a hinge joint, movement occurs primarily in one plane. Reason: The bone ends are shaped to allow sliding in all directions.

(iii) (A) is true, but (R) is false. A hinge joint restricts movement to one plane (bending and straightening). The reason is false because bone ends in a hinge joint are shaped to interlock and allow motion in only one direction, not sliding in all directions like a ball and socket joint.

items.stem: Plot a graph between the age of a tree (in years) on the x-axis and the diameter of the tree (in cm) along with the number of annual rings formed over time on the y-axis, using the data given in the Table. S. No. Age of Teak Tree (Years) DBH (cm) Number of Annual Rings 1 5 4 5 2 10 8 10 3 20 24 20 4 25 28 25 5 30 32 30 6 40 40 40 Tissues in Action (i) Analyse the graph in terms of the diameter of the stem over time and share the interpretation. (ii) What is the relation between the diameter of the teak tree to the annual rings formed? (iii) Which specialised tissue is responsible for the girth of the stem and where is it located?
items.answer: (i) (ii) There is a direct proportionality between the diameter of the teak tree and the number of annual rings formed. As the number of annual rings increases (representing each year of growth), the diameter of the tree correspondingly increases, demonstrating that each ring adds a new layer to the tree’s overall girth. (iii) The lateral meristem is the specialised tissue responsible for increasing the girth or diameter of the stem. It is located along the circumference of the stems and roots, forming concentric rings of actively dividing cells.

items.stem: In a forest, it was observed that one of the trees was severely debarked by an elephant to meet its food requirements, as the bark is a rich source of nutrients Figure. Based on your learning, answer the following: (i) Which function(s) of the tree is/are hampered by debarking? (ii) Which plant tissue would be affected by further damage to the tree trunk even after debarking? (iii) Which function of the tree would be hampered if the tissues beneath the bark were severely damaged? (iv) What assumptions are you making to answer the questions above? How would the answer change if your assumptions are also changed?
items.answer: (i) Debarking removes the outer protective epidermal/cork layers and the inner phloem tissue. This severely hampers the tree’s protective function against water loss, mechanical injury, and infections. More critically, the removal of phloem disrupts the downward transport of food produced in the leaves to the roots and lower trunk. (ii) Further damage to the deeper layers of the tree trunk after the outer bark and phloem are removed would affect the xylem tissue, which constitutes the woody core of the trunk. (iii) If the xylem tissues lying beneath the bark were severely damaged, the upward transport of water and dissolved minerals from the roots to the leaves would be hampered. This would quickly lead to wilting and the inability of leaves to perform photosynthesis. (iv) The primary assumption made is that debarking removes the complete ring of outer bark and the underlying living phloem tissue (girdling), while leaving the deeper xylem intact initially. If the assumption is changed to mean only superficial dead cork cells were scraped off without damaging the phloem, then food transport would not be hampered, and the tree could heal. If the assumption is that the damage was deep enough to sever both phloem and xylem simultaneously, then both food and water transport would instantly stop, causing rapid death of the entire plant.

items.stem: Aamrapali observed that a young mango sapling’s stem bends flexibly during monsoon winds and does not break. Which tissue is responsible for this flexibility? Predict and provide your explanation of the impact if the existing tissue was replaced by sclerenchyma.
items.answer: The collenchyma tissue is responsible for the flexibility observed in the young mango sapling’s stem, allowing it to bend under stress without breaking. If the collenchyma were replaced by sclerenchyma, the stem would lose its elasticity and become completely hard, rigid, and brittle. Under the strong force of monsoon winds, the stiff stem would be unable to bend and would likely snap and break, because sclerenchyma provides rigid mechanical support due to its thick lignified walls, lacking the flexible nature of collenchyma.

items.stem: Sohan designed an experiment for the regeneration of sugarcane, where he used cuttings to grow sugarcane. He used two types of cuttings, type ‘A’ and type ‘B’ . After a few weeks, type ‘B’ cuttings sprouted and developed into sugarcane plants, whereas the type ‘A’ cuttings did not sprout. (i) Why were the type ‘B’ cuttings able to grow as sugarcane but type ‘A’ could not? (ii) What difference was present in type ‘B’ compared to type ‘A’? (iii) What observation or measurement was made to determine whether this change had an effect? (iv) What parameters should be kept the same for both types of cuttings to ensure a fair comparison?
items.answer: (i) Based on the visual reference in figure, type ‘B’ cuttings contain nodes, whereas type ‘A’ cuttings are only internodal sections. Type ‘B’ cuttings were able to grow because the nodes contain intercalary meristematic tissues, whose actively dividing cells are essential for sprouting new shoots and roots. Type ‘A’ could not grow as it lacked these meristematic regions. (ii) The crucial structural difference is the presence of nodes (the joint-like structures) in type ‘B’ cuttings and their absence in type ‘A’ cuttings. These nodes house the intercalary meristem necessary for regeneration. (iii) The primary observation made to determine the effect was visually checking whether the planted cuttings sprouted new shoots and developed into visible sugarcane plants after a period of a few weeks. (iv) To ensure a fair scientific comparison, external growth parameters such as soil type, moisture level, amount of sunlight, ambient temperature, and the source plant’s age and health should be kept identical for both type ‘A’ and type ‘B’ cuttings.

items.stem: During the discussion in class, Rohan gives a statement that, “A tissue is a group of similar cells performing similar functions”. But Rajiv counter argues that, “this is true in case of simple tissues but little different in case of complex tissues”. Provide your explanation in view of the discussion in class.
items.answer: Rajiv’s counter-argument is scientifically correct. Rohan’s definition perfectly describes simple tissues, such as parenchyma or epithelial tissue, where all constituent cells are structurally similar and carry out identical functions. However, complex tissues in plants, like xylem and phloem, are composed of more than one distinct type of cell that work together as a cohesive unit to perform a common overall function. For example, xylem consists of structurally different tracheids, vessels, parenchyma, and fibres that all coordinate to transport water, making the definition of a tissue broader when considering complex types.

items.stem: Coconut husk fibres are used for mats which are tough and fibrous. Which tissue has structural features suitable for providing this strength? Explain why living parenchyma couldn’t serve the same purpose.
items.answer: Sclerenchyma tissue has the structural features suitable for providing the tough, fibrous strength seen in coconut husks. Its cells are dead, long, and have exceptionally thick walls due to the heavy deposition of lignin, making them rigid and strong. Living parenchyma could not serve this purpose because its cells have thin walls made only of cellulose, remain soft, and are structurally adapted for functions like food storage and photosynthesis rather than providing high tensile mechanical strength. items.stem: Vibha claims to her friend Neha that, “Meristematic cells are located only at the root and shoot apices”. What do you think about this statement? What question can Neha ask Vibha to help her understand further if the statement is incorrect?
items.answer: Vibha’s statement is incorrect because meristematic tissues are not restricted only to the tips of roots and shoots. They are also found as lateral meristems (cambium) along the sides of stems and roots, and as intercalary meristems at the nodes or bases of leaves. To help Vibha realize this, Neha could ask: “If meristematic cells are only at the very tips for increasing length, which cells are responsible for a tree trunk growing wider in girth over the years, or how does a lawn grass regrow its leaves after being mowed from the middle?”

items.stem: A plant cell and an animal cell are of the same size. (i) Which cell will have a larger vacuole? Give reasons. (ii) What assumptions are you making to answer the question above?
items.answer: (i) The plant cell will have a significantly larger vacuole. Plant cells typically feature a single, large central vacuole that can occupy most of the cell’s volume to store water, essential nutrients, and waste products, while also providing necessary turgidity to maintain the plant’s rigid structure. In contrast, animal cells either lack vacuoles entirely or have very small, temporary ones. (ii) The primary assumption made is that we are comparing a mature, fully differentiated plant cell (like a typical parenchyma cell) with a standard mature animal cell. Young meristematic plant cells might have smaller vacuoles resembling animal cells, so the generalization assumes typical adult cell structures.

items.stem: A textbook states, “Each plant tissue performs only one specific function”. What questions would you ask to critically examine the correctness of this statement? What examples of tissues would you take to find out the answers to these questions?
items.answer: To critically examine this statement, I would ask: “Can a specific plant tissue adapt to perform multiple physiological roles depending on its location in the plant body?” and “Do basic tissues have specialized variations that handle completely different tasks?” To find the answers, I would examine parenchyma tissue. While basic parenchyma primarily stores food, specialized parenchyma in leaves contains chlorophyll to perform photosynthesis (chlorenchyma), and in aquatic plants, it develops large air spaces to provide buoyancy (aerenchyma). This demonstrates that a single fundamental tissue category can be modified to perform several entirely distinct and specific functions, proving the textbook statement incorrect. OBJECTIVE QUESTION
